title: 'What Works' in Reading Comprehension--And What Doesn't
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler critiques a What Works Clearinghouse practice guide on interventions for struggling readers in grades four to nine, arguing that it ignores cognitive science. She says the guide lumps decoding, fluency and comprehension together, though comprehension is tied to general learning, where prior knowledge frees working memory. The guide's idea of building word and world knowledge amounts to brief pre-teaching of terms, and its emphasis on skills like generating gist statements across varied topics repeats ineffective classroom practice. She argues these strategies work only in service of a coherent knowledge-building curriculum. As a counterpoint she cites English studies where teachers read novels aloud for about thirty minutes a day and students made large gains, suggesting it as a simpler, enjoyable approach.
points: Reading comprehension is inseparable from general learning, so research on it should draw on cognitive science and not stay within reading research.
Prior knowledge relieves working memory, so one-off explanations of unfamiliar words before reading will not build lasting comprehension.
Practicing skills such as finding the main idea on random topics yields little unless embedded in a coherent, knowledge-building curriculum.
The guide's advice to vary topics and to use harder text conflicts with its acknowledgment that missing knowledge impedes comprehension.
Reported English read-aloud studies showed striking gains and could free schedule time for history and science.
quotes: Research in education rarely draws on the substantial body of scientific evidence on how learning works. That’s a problem for teachers, students—and the rest of us.

But reading comprehension is different. It’s not just a reading process. It’s inextricably connected to the process of learning in general. And cognitive scientists have found that the key factor in learning new information is how much relevant information you already have.

That’s because the aspect of our consciousness that takes in new information, our “working memory,” is easily overwhelmed. Until we become fluent readers, we have to juggle things in working memory like how to decode unfamiliar words and where to put the emphasis in sentences, in addition to the new information in the text. The more information we have in long-term memory that’s relevant to the text—whether that’s knowledge of the topic or general academic vocabulary, or both—the more capacity we have in working memory to understand and retain new information.

The theory has long been that students just need to practice this skill and get better at it. But it’s often either so obvious that students won’t need much practice—just look at the title and circle the words that appear in the text frequently, as the guide recommends—or too difficult to accomplish without a base of relevant prior knowledge.

It's not that the practices the guide recommends are ineffective, per se. They’re only ineffective when they’re viewed as ends in themselves—skills that can be acquired in the abstract and applied generally. If they’re used in service of helping students understand the content of a coherent, knowledge-building curriculum—which unfortunately isn’t the kind used in most schools—they can be quite effective, particularly when combined with carefully sequenced writing instruction.

Teachers read aloud novels that exceeded students’ own reading abilities for about 30 minutes a day, leading class discussions at the end of each chapter, for 12 weeks. In an initial experiment with 12- and 13-year-olds, poor readers made 16 months of progress in that time, as measured by a standardized reading comprehension test.

Just reading novels won’t provide all the knowledge kids need to understand complex text in areas like history and science. But if we spent only half an hour a day reading novels aloud—instead of the two or three hours many schools spend on reading comprehension skills—we’d have lots more time in the schedule for history and science.
